title: Lower yields are not an earnings guarantee.
deck: My read after Thursday’s close: a lower discount rate cannot by itself protect an equity valuation. Technology weakness contrasted with gains elsewhere, while the latest claims data offered reassurance about layoffs but less certainty about finding work. Keep earnings assumptions separate from the interest-rate story.

sections.title: Lower bond yields did not lift every stock.
sections.body: AP reported a 1.3% Nasdaq Composite decline and a 0.1% Dow gain; most S&P 500 constituents rose despite the index’s fall. Treasury’s two-year par yield eased to 4.75% from 4.77%, ten years to 5.22% from 5.28%, and thirty years to 5.60% from 5.67%. My interpretation: this was not a uniform risk-off session, and lower yields alone were insufficient to offset equity-specific concerns. The countercase is that rotation can leave the broader market healthier than the headline index suggests. One session cannot settle that question or establish why yields moved; subsequent earnings and participation matter.

sections.title: Few new claims do not measure the ease of getting hired.
sections.body: The Labor Department’s 8 October release showed initial claims down 2,000 to 197,000 for the week ended 3 October. The four-week average was 198,000. Continuing claims rose 17,000 to 1,716,000 for the earlier week ended 26 September. My assessment: new benefit applications do not signal a sudden layoff surge, but the continuing-claims rise warrants watching. It does not alone prove weaker hiring: eligibility, benefit duration and weekly noise also matter. The bullish counterargument is that the continuing-claims four-week average fell to 1,711,000. I would wait for persistence and corroborating employment data before reducing a company’s long-run demand forecast.

sections.title: A policy risk is not a scheduled outcome.
sections.body: Minutes released on 7 October describe the September 15–16 meeting, not a new rate decision. At that meeting, the Fed raised its target range by a quarter percentage point to 3.75–4.00%. Most participants then thought another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end, while emphasizing incoming information. My inference: financing assumptions should retain an upside-rate scenario, but the minutes do not commit the Fed to a particular next move. The competing case is that subsequent evidence could justify patience. Thursday’s claims figures are newer than the meeting; they inform the current debate but were not information participants had at the time.

sections.title: Separate cheaper capital from weaker cash flows.
sections.body: In the DCF, first lower WACC with cash flows unchanged; then reduce free-cash-flow growth while keeping WACC fixed. Finally combine them. This makes it clear whether a valuation depends more on financing relief or operating delivery. Do not map a daily Treasury change mechanically into WACC: equity risk and credit spreads can move differently. In the LBO Deal Lab, compare lower growth against higher borrowing costs with the exit multiple unchanged. Its constant-rate scenarios are not floating-rate forecasts. Sustained cash-flow delivery alongside cheaper financing would strengthen the optimistic case; weaker margins or cash conversion could overwhelm the benefit of lower yields.

watch: Look for sustained participation beyond technology, and compare earnings guidance with actual cash conversion rather than assuming a lower yield guarantees higher equity prices.
Watch revisions and the next several claims releases. Initial and continuing claims cover different weeks and should not be treated as a direct hiring statistic.
Separate fresh inflation and employment releases from September’s policy deliberations before changing financing assumptions.
